notes.b: Where a home is built shapes the household's daily life and costs for years. The choice depends on how suitable the site is, what the household needs and what the site costs. A local authority is the county or city council, and its development plan sets how land in the area may be used.
points: Urban or rural setting: urban sites give shops, transport, services and jobs, but cost more and offer less space. Rural sites give space, quiet and a lower land price, but may need a private water supply and a wastewater treatment system, and mean longer travel.
Proximity to family, work, schools, childcare, shops, health services and public transport affects the daily time and cost of travel, and the ease of family life.
Ground conditions: a stable soil structure, good slope and drainage and freedom from flood risk are checked by a site survey before building, because a poor site can damage the house later.
Shelter from wind matters, and so does the absence of risks nearby such as pollution, pylons, factories or landfill.
Aspect (the direction the site faces) and orientation of the house determine how much daylight and solar heat it receives. They also affect privacy and views.
Services available: electricity, water, sewerage, gas, broadband and refuse collection, plus the cost of connecting them, which adds to the real price of a site.

Budget and value: the price of the site and the cost of connecting services limit the location a household can afford. Future developments in the area affect the prospects for the value of the property.

Building and planning regulations, including the development plan, can restrict where and how a house may be built. In a case study, apply all these factors to the needs of the family described to choose the location, house design, interior and services.
notes.tip: For a case-study family, apply aspect, services, proximity, budget and the family's own needs to the particular family described, not just list factors.

notes.b: Once a site is chosen, the style of house must suit the family, the site and the budget. A house that suits one family can be a poor fit for another.
points: House style is chosen by comparing traditional and modern designs, and bungalow and two-storey layouts, against the family's budget.
The size, stage (age group) and lifestyle of the family determine the number of bedrooms, the amount of living space and the need for storage, because a growing family needs more of each.
Special needs, such as a wheelchair user, may require a single-storey house, step-free access and wider doors so that the person can move around independently.
Potential to convert the attic, extend the house or add a garage must be checked against planning rules for the area, so that future changes are allowed.
Personal taste and the style of neighbouring houses determine whether a design fits its surroundings.
notes.tip: In a case-study question, tie each style choice to the family's size, needs and budget, for example a single-storey house with step-free access for a wheelchair user.

notes.b: There are two kinds of permission, and they differ in how much detail the applicant must supply and in what each one settles. Outline permission is a first check on the idea. Full permission is the approval needed to build.
points: Planning permission from the local authority is required for most building work unless the development is exempt under the planning regulations, for example some small extensions.
Outline permission establishes whether the planning authority agrees in principle to a development, before detailed plans are prepared. It is not permission to build.

An outline application needs only a site map showing the location and layout of the proposed house, with basic details of the proposal, not detailed house plans. This saves the cost of drawing full plans for a site that may be refused.
Full permission requires detailed plans and drawings, the site layout, house plans, elevations and finishes, details of water supply and drainage, and the materials to be used in construction.
Full permission also requires the appropriate fee, copies of the public notices (newspaper and site notice) and the position of the site notice.
A person who is granted outline permission must still get full permission (detailed approval) before building.
notes.tip: Outline permission is not permission to build, and it is not a short form of full permission. The difference is the level of detail required and what it settles, so say both.

notes.b: The procedure for full permission is set in the Planning and Development Act 2024. It follows a fixed order so that the public can see and comment on a proposal before the council decides. Learn the order of the steps.
points: 1. Optional first step: hold a pre-planning meeting with the planning authority to discuss the proposal before applying, and prepare drawings with an architect.
2. Publish a notice of intention to apply in a local newspaper, and erect a site notice on the proposed site, so that neighbours and the public are told.

3. Lodge the application with the local authority: the application form, the site maps, the house plans and drawings, the materials, a copy of the notices and the fee. The authority acknowledges receipt.
4. The application is placed on the planning register, where members of the public can inspect it and lodge a written submission or objection.
5. Planning officials inspect the site and examine the plans against the development plan before a decision is made. The authority may ask for further information.
6. The authority grants permission, often with conditions, or refuses it. If permission is refused, the applicant must be given the reasons.

7. Appeals against the decision of the planning authority are made to An Coimisiún Pleanála, which replaced An Bord Pleanála in June 2025. An applicant who is refused, or a person who objected, may appeal. If nobody appeals, permission is confirmed.
Diagram: a flowchart of the sequence from the pre-planning meeting and the notices through to the decision and the appeal route.
notes.tip: This is asked almost every year, so give a numbered sequence: newspaper and site notices, lodging with plans and fee, the planning register and public inspection, site inspection, the decision with reasons for refusal, and the appeal route. A pre-planning meeting can also earn credit. Appeals go to An Coimisiún Pleanála, not An Bord Pleanála.

notes.b: Planning control is the system that decides what may be built and where. Without it, anyone could build anything anywhere, so permission is needed for most building work.
points: Developments must fit in with the local development plan for the area, which is how the council plans land use.
Houses must not be built so that they overlook neighbours, which protects their privacy.
Industrial factories must not be built in residential areas, so that homes are kept away from noise and pollution.
Scenic areas, tourist attractions and old buildings are protected, so scenic areas have restrictions on house building.
New houses must conform to the style of others in the area, and property values are protected.
Services and infrastructure are planned, so that roads, water and sewerage can cope with new development.
notes.tip: If asked why planning permission is needed, give separate reasons such as fitting the development plan, keeping factories away from houses, protecting scenery and old buildings, and protecting neighbours.

notes.b: Building a house involves legal, technical and practical work that most families cannot do themselves. Each professional has a separate role, and exam marks go to the specific role, not to a vague statement that they help with the house.
points: Architect: advises on the site and design, prepares plans and drawings from the family's brief and budget, prepares and submits the planning application, advises on builders and materials, and may supervise construction.
Engineer (structural or site engineer): advises on the structure and foundations, supervises structural work and solves building problems.

Surveyor: surveys the site and building, checks boundaries and defects, identifies potential problem areas and recommends how to deal with them before they affect the building. A quantity surveyor estimates and controls costs, and a surveyor may draw up a snag list of faults before final payment.

Solicitor: handles the legal side, including contracts, checking title deeds, rights of way (checked with the Land Registry), registering ownership, legal advice on building and planning regulations and loan paperwork.

Builder: agrees the price and completion date in a contract, prepares the site, manages subcontractors such as electricians, plumbers, plasterers and tilers, follows the drawings and rectifies faults.
Other services include interior designers, landscape architects, electricians, plumbers and BER assessors. An interior designer brings expertise and access to suppliers, but at a cost.

A book of house plans is a catalogue of ready-drawn designs. It is cheaper than commissioning an architect, but the plans are not tailored to the site or the family, must still be submitted for planning permission and often need an architect or engineer to adapt them to the site.
notes.tip: Architect, engineer, solicitor, surveyor and builder are the standard five, so give specific roles: for example, draws plans, applies for permission and may supervise beats helps with the house. An architect designs, an engineer advises on structure, a surveyor inspects and reports, a builder constructs and a solicitor deals with law. A book of house plans is not a substitute for planning permission.

keyTerms.definition: Approval from the local authority that is required before most house building or extension work may begin.
A preliminary approval, based on a site map, which shows whether the planning authority agrees in principle to a development.
Approval given on detailed plans, drawings and specifications, after public notice and consideration of objections.
A notice displayed on the proposed site to inform the public that a planning application has been made.
The public record kept by the local authority of planning applications, which members of the public may inspect.
The direction a site or house faces, which determines the daylight and solar heat it receives.
A professional who surveys a site or building, identifies problems and recommends solutions.
Documents proving legal ownership of a property, checked by a solicitor during a purchase.
The builder's final rectification of faults and unfinished work before a house is handed over.
A set of pre-drawn house designs that a buyer can purchase at lower cost than an architect's design.

factCards.term: What an outline application must include
factCards.definition: A site map showing the location and layout of the proposed house, without detailed house plans.

factCards.term: Four details a full application must contain
factCards.definition: Detailed plans with elevations and finishes; site layout with water supply and drainage; copies of the public notices; the fee and details of materials.

factCards.term: Three reasons a house needs approval before building
factCards.definition: To make sure houses fit the local development plan; to stop houses overlooking neighbours; to keep factories out of residential areas.

factCards.term: Body that hears appeals against a planning decision
factCards.definition: An Coimisiún Pleanála, which replaced An Bord Pleanála in June 2025.

factCards.term: Role of the site and building survey professional
factCards.definition: To survey the site and building, identify problem areas and recommend solutions before they affect the structure.

factCards.term: Three tasks of a solicitor in a house purchase
factCards.definition: Checking the title deeds; checking rights of way with the Land Registry; advising on building and planning regulations.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between outline planning permission and full planning permission.
questions.model: Outline permission establishes whether the planning authority agrees in principle to the development. It needs only a site map showing the location and layout, not detailed house plans. Full permission needs detailed plans and drawings, site layout with water supply and drainage details, the fee, copies of the public notices and the materials to be used. Full permission is the decision that allows building to begin.

questions.prompt: Discuss the professional services a family would use when building a new house, and explain the role each one plays.
questions.model: Architect: advises on site and design, prepares plans and drawings, applies for planning permission and may oversee construction. Engineer: advises on the structure, supervises structural work and solves building problems. Surveyor: surveys the site and building, identifies problem areas and recommends solutions. Solicitor: handles contracts, title deeds, rights of way and legal advice on building and planning regulations. Builder: agrees price and timescale, prepares the site, manages subcontractors and rectifies faults. Other services include interior designers, electricians, plumbers and BER assessors. Each professional should be linked to the stage at which they are needed, and the answer should explain how the services work together to produce a house that meets planning and building standards.
